title: Polygon Triangulation
notes: Open the lecture by presenting triangulation as the chapter's central translation: a simple polygon becomes a finite set of triangles, and that decomposition supports both the art gallery theorem and a concrete C-style algorithm. The source span should remain visible as printed pages 1-43, with the provenance note that the repository coverage maps those printed pages to PDF pages 10-52.

title: Chapter Map
notes: Use the chain across the slide as the lecture route. First we agree on what a polygon is and what its inside means. Then visibility gives diagonals, diagonals give triangulations, triangulations give proof structures, and the final third of the chapter turns all of that into orientation, intersection, InCone, and ear clipping code.

title: What Counts As A Polygon
notes: Slow down here because many later tests silently assume this contract. A simple polygon is a closed cyclic boundary that does not cross itself, so every edge has a previous and next edge and the curve separates inside from outside. The self-intersecting example is not a different input style; it violates the object the triangulation theorem is about.

title: Visibility And Guarding
notes: Introduce visibility as a segment-inside-polygon question. Two points see each other when the open segment between them stays in the polygon's interior, with boundary endpoint conventions handled separately. The guard formulation is then natural: choose vertices or points whose visibility regions cover the polygon, and triangulation will soon make that coverage finite.

title: Why floor(n/3) Appears
notes: The art gallery bound should feel surprising before it becomes formal. The comb picture suggests why every third notch can force a new guard, while the small n cases remind students that the formula is a worst-case ceiling, not a claim that every polygon needs that many guards. This prepares the class for Fisk's coloring proof.

title: Fisk's Proof In Four Moves
notes: Present Fisk's proof as a compressed algorithmic certificate. Triangulate the polygon, 3-color the triangulation graph, choose the smallest color class, and observe that every triangle has all three colors. Since the triangles cover the polygon, the chosen color class sees the whole polygon, and pigeonhole gives the floor n over 3 bound.

title: Diagonals And Triangulations
notes: Define a legal diagonal with both global and local responsibilities. It connects nonadjacent vertices, avoids crossing boundary edges, and lies inside the polygon near both endpoints. The contrast between the blue diagonal and the amber crossing segment sets up why a triangulation is a maximal noncrossing collection, not merely several attractive chords.

title: Existence Of A Diagonal
notes: Sketch the proof move rather than treating existence as magic. Pick a convex vertex and test the chord between its neighbors. If that chord is clear, it is a diagonal. If it is blocked, the blocking vertex inside the candidate triangle gives a smaller local choice that yields a diagonal. This is the proof's constructive heartbeat.

title: Counting Triangles And Diagonals
notes: Make the two counting formulas feel inevitable from a split. One diagonal divides an n-gon into two smaller polygons whose sizes overlap at the diagonal endpoints. Induction then gives T(n)=n-2 triangles and D(n)=n-3 internal diagonals. The notebook's checked eight-vertex polygon produces six triangles and five diagonals, matching the formulas.

title: Dual Tree And Two Ears
notes: Translate the triangulation into graph language. Each triangle becomes a node, and shared diagonals become edges of the weak dual. Because the dual is a tree, it has leaves; leaf triangles touch the rest of the triangulation along one diagonal and therefore are ears. The notebook example has six dual nodes, five dual edges, and four leaf ears.

title: Three-Coloring And Fisk Guards
notes: Show the coloring as a maintained invariant on the triangulation graph. Every triangle receives one vertex of each color, so placing guards on any one color class covers every triangle. The checked notebook polygon selects color 2 with vertices 1 and 5, which is within floor of eight over three and makes the guard theorem concrete.

title: Signed Area Is The Predicate Engine
notes: Connect area, orientation, and implementation in one formula. The shoelace sum gives the polygon's signed area and confirms counterclockwise orientation when positive. The same determinant, restricted to three points, drives left-turn tests. The notebook check reports area 5.44 and equal triangle-fan area, making area conservation a testable invariant.

title: From Slopes To Orientation Predicates
notes: Warn students away from slope comparisons without making the point only numerical. Slopes need special vertical cases and become fragile near parallel lines, while the determinant gives one sign convention for left, right, and collinear triples. This is why the C vocabulary in the chapter is built around area2, left, left_on, collinear, and between.

title: Segment Intersection Test Board
notes: Use the four cases as a diagnostic board for the predicate layer. Proper crossing, endpoint touch, collinear overlap, and disjoint segments should not be collapsed if a downstream routine cares about boundary conventions. Diagonal testing usually wants to reject boundary crossings while still allowing the proposed diagonal to meet the polygon at its own endpoints.

title: Diagonal Testing
notes: Separate the diagonal test into the two questions the implementation asks. Globally, the candidate segment must avoid all unrelated polygon edges. Locally, the InCone test checks that the chord leaves each endpoint through the interior wedge, with reflex vertices reversing the intuitive picture. Both parts are needed before an ear is safe to clip.

title: Ear Clipping As Algorithmic Proof
notes: Close by making the algorithm look like the proof running in a loop. Find a convex empty ear, record its diagonal or final triangle, remove the ear tip, and repeat. A straightforward implementation scans candidates at each removal, giving O(n^2) time. The chapter's theorem-level checks then become program checks: n-2 triangles, n-3 diagonals, and conserved area.
